title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is dominated by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation over reported affairs, including one with a woman US authorities suspect of spying for China, along with the questions that follow about his successor, chip exports and national security. Also covered: a long Microsoft 365 outage, a narrow Democratic win in the Kansas governor's race, a challenge to Chuck Schumer's Senate leadership, US seizures tied to North Korea's Binance hack, and Korean and Charlotte-area local news.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after reported affairs, including one with suspected Chinese spy
stories.summary: Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it for 33 years, resigned Thursday as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. His exit followed reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom US authorities suspect of spying for China, and one with a direct report. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones becomes the board's first chair. On Sunday the board had expressed confidence in Huang while opening an independent investigation into whether national security or company secrets were compromised. The case has prompted calls in Congress for tighter chip export controls and for answers from Huang, Nvidia and the Trump administration.
key_facts: Huang, 63, stepped down Thursday; Colette Kress, CFO since 2013, is interim CEO and keeps her finance role.
Nvidia shares fell more than 10% in US premarket trading Thursday.
Nvidia says it has no reason to believe national security or its confidential information was compromised; China denies Alice Huang was a spy.
House Speaker Mike Johnson cited a 'developing consensus in Congress' on limiting chip exports to China.
Nvidia says its quarterly earnings report will go ahead as scheduled on Nov. 17.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and PBS focused on national security and accountability. They quoted Democrats Chuck Schumer, who asked what President Trump knew when he invited Huang aboard Air Force One, and Hakeem Jeffries, who is demanding a classified briefing. They also covered bipartisan pressure for chip export curbs. PBS guest Dmitri Alperovitch argued the larger issue is possible illegal chip smuggling to China, not Huang's private life.

The Korea Herald and Axios took a corporate-governance and business angle: the board's reversal, the succession search, the share drop, reassurances about operations, and what it means for Nvidia's Korean suppliers Samsung and SK hynix.

Fox Business framed it mainly as an investor story, quoting analysts who called Kress a 'steady hand' while warning that losing Huang's vision and dealmaking is a major risk. Reason's podcast treated it more lightly, describing Huang as having been 'honeypotted.'

disputed: Whether Alice Huang was in fact a spy, and whether any Nvidia secrets were compromised, has not been established.

Accounts differ on who first reported the relationship with an Nvidia employee and when: the Korea Herald cites a New York Times report on Wednesday, while Reason cites a Reuters report after the resignation.
Fox Business described Huang's exit as a board 'ouster'; other outlets called it a resignation.
Reports that Huang will testify before Congress are still developing (see s2).
stories.why: Nvidia makes the chips behind the AI boom, so its leadership and any security breach affect markets, US-China tech policy and the wider AI industry.

stories.headline: Trump suggests Tim Cook should succeed Huang as Nvidia CEO
stories.summary: Shortly after Huang resigned, President Trump wrote on Truth Social that 'there is only one man' to replace him: Apple executive chairman and former CEO Tim Cook, adding 'A Legend replaces a Legend!' On a podcast, Trump repeated the idea and said Huang called him and is 'going through hell.' He said whether Huang should have resigned depends on whether the woman was a spy, which he said he did not know had been determined. There is no indication Cook is interested, and Nvidia's board says it will consider internal and external candidates.
key_facts: Trump posted on Truth Social Thursday: 'there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple.'
Cook stepped down as Apple CEO on Sept. 1, 2026, and became executive chairman; John Ternus is Apple's CEO.
Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld had separately suggested Cook as a candidate in a Time op-ed.
Trump said Monday he believed Huang's account that he did not know of the woman's alleged intelligence ties.

perspectives.framing: The Verge quoted Trump's podcast remarks at length, including his sympathy for Huang. It noted Cook's close relationship with Trump, citing a gold statue Cook gave him and a Trump post about Apple's head calling to 'kiss my ass.'

TechCrunch, Axios and The Hill reported the suggestion with some skepticism. Axios said it was unclear whether Trump was joking and noted he did not address the controversy. TechCrunch added Sonnenfeld's similar view.

Fox Business reported the endorsement straight and stressed that no evidence has publicly shown Huang disclosed secrets. The Daily Caller added harder claims: a DOJ probe of Alice Huang over Super Micro smuggling (via a social media post citing Bloomberg), an allegation that she helped move more than $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China, and that Huang agreed to testify before the House Foreign Affairs Committee before Thanksgiving.

disputed: Whether Trump's suggestion was serious, and whether Cook has any interest.
The Daily Caller's claims about $7.5 billion in chips moved to China and a DOJ probe were not reported by other outlets here.
Huang's congressional testimony: The Guardian says he is 'expected' to testify; the Daily Caller says he agreed to appear before Thanksgiving.
Nvidia's market value: TechCrunch puts it at about $3.8 trillion; the Daily Caller says it fell below $4 trillion.
stories.why: A president publicly weighing in on a private company's CEO pick is unusual and adds political pressure to Nvidia's succession.

stories.headline: Microsoft 365 outage disrupts Outlook, Teams and other services for hours
stories.summary: A Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday afternoon cut off access to Outlook and Exchange Online for many users and also affected Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and other services. Microsoft said a number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, overloading the rest of its infrastructure. It paused deployments, rerouted traffic and restarted servers. By evening it reported only limited recovery and was weighing whether to roll back recent configuration updates, with no estimate for full restoration. The outage also broke Microsoft connectors used by OpenAI and Anthropic.
key_facts: Downdetector logged nearly 130,000 Outlook reports at the peak around 1 p.m. ET.
Microsoft says the incident began at 1:26 p.m. ET; a separate Teams outage earlier that day (9:45 to 10:53 a.m. ET) was resolved.
A Microsoft spokesperson said the company had 'no indication of a cyber-attack.'
The disruption lasted more than five hours, with only partial recovery reported by about 6 p.m. ET.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and The Verge followed Microsoft's technical updates closely. The Guardian quoted RMIT's Mark Gregory, who described a 'cascading problem' likely caused by a network misconfiguration and urged better testing and backup plans. It also noted a separate Azure outage last month.

BleepingComputer and DW gave detailed technical timelines. WSOC centered on Charlotte workers who could not send email, and quoted an expert who said Microsoft had not clearly ruled out malicious activity, though that does not mean an attack occurred.
The Washington Examiner gave a brief factual account focused on the number of affected users.

disputed: The root cause is not confirmed. Microsoft cited unavailable servers and possibly recent configuration changes; an outside expert suggested a network-layer misconfiguration.
Start times differ: around noon (WSOC), just before 1 p.m. (The Verge), and 1:26 p.m. ET (Microsoft).
Whether the earlier Teams incident is related is unknown.
DW described the outage as mainly in the US; others said users in any region could be affected.
stories.why: Huge numbers of businesses depend on Microsoft's cloud tools, so outages like this can halt everyday work.

stories.headline: Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim CEO
stories.summary: Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO since 2013, is now interim CEO while the board searches for Huang's permanent successor. In emails to staff, Kress thanked employees for their resilience during an 'extraordinarily difficult period' and announced a company meeting on Nov. 18. Board chair Harvey Jones said the board has 'full confidence' in her. Analysts see her as a familiar, trusted figure, though some doubt she would get the job permanently, and names floated as successors include Chris Malachowsky, Ian Buck, Tim Cook and Arm's Rene Haas.
key_facts: Kress is 59 and previously worked at Texas Instruments, Microsoft (1997 to 2010) and Cisco.
Forbes estimates her net worth at about $1.2 billion.
Nvidia's revenue grew from $4.13 billion in the fiscal year she joined to $215.9 billion in fiscal 2026.
An all-company meeting is set for Nov. 18 at 9 a.m. PT.

perspectives.framing: CNBC published the internal staff emails in full. BBC and TechCrunch profiled Kress and surveyed possible successors, citing analysts who suggest the company may eventually want an engineer as CEO.

Fox Business focused on her personal fortune and career path. It noted that Nvidia's at-will employment means executives can be fired without pre-negotiated severance, and referred to the board's 'ouster' of Huang.

disputed: Who will become permanent CEO, and whether Kress is a serious candidate for the role.
stories.why: Kress's first test comes with the Nov. 17 earnings report, when investors will judge Nvidia's stability without Huang.

stories.headline: Democrat Cindy Holscher wins Kansas governor's race
stories.summary: Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher defeated Republican Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson, who was endorsed by Trump, to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly. The Associated Press called the race Thursday, two days after Election Day. Holscher campaigned on a moratorium on new AI data centers, support for public schools over vouchers, and legalizing cannabis. Masterson focused on property tax cuts. He conceded, and he will return to the GOP-controlled state Senate.
key_facts: The Washington Examiner reported Holscher leading 50.3% to 49.7% when AP called the race.
Trump won Kansas by 16 points in 2024.
PBS/AP reported the Republican Governors Association spent $19 million on ads, and Republicans outspent Democrats more than 3 to 1 overall.
It is the third straight Kansas governor's race won by a Democrat.

perspectives.framing: PBS/AP and NPR framed the win as part of a national Democratic wave, alongside other Kansas Democratic victories for US Senate and attorney general. They highlighted her populist and data-center messaging and how heavily Republicans outspent her.
The Hill described it as denying Republicans one of their best pickup chances this year.

Fox News stressed that Democrats keep winning Kansas governor's races despite the state's Republican lean. It noted scrutiny of Holscher's 2023 posts suggesting Jesus could have been transgender, and highlighted Masterson's concession and continued GOP control of the legislature.

stories.why: A Democratic win in a strongly Republican state, by a candidate who ran against AI data centers, is a sign of the national political mood after the midterms.

stories.headline: Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
stories.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced Thursday that he will challenge Chuck Schumer for majority leader when Democrats take control of the Senate in January. Van Hollen said voters called for change and that the party needs 'new leadership.' Schumer replied within a minute that he has the votes to remain leader, pointing to '55 seats and counting.' Senate Democrats will choose their leader by secret ballot on Dec. 1.
key_facts: The leadership vote is a secret ballot on Dec. 1.
Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats since 2017; Van Hollen, 67, has been in Congress since 2003.
Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan endorsed Van Hollen.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian framed the race as progressive versus centrist and as a choice about how forcefully to confront Trump. It pointed to Van Hollen's 2025 trip to El Salvador over a wrongly deported constituent, and covered El-Sayed's endorsement and his primary win over Schumer's preferred candidate.
Axios highlighted the nearly three-week window for activists to pressure senators, and the Democratic divisions the race exposes despite the party's midterm success.

Fox News called Van Hollen a 'progressive darling,' noted his criticism that Schumer favored the crypto industry and AIPAC over progressive candidates, and pointed to Bernie Sanders saying he won't back Schumer. The Washington Examiner cited a 'growing chorus' of Democrats seeking new leadership.

disputed: Schumer's claim that he has the votes to stay leader is unverified.
stories.why: The winner will lead the new Senate majority and shape how Democrats handle the Trump administration.

stories.headline: US freezes and seizes funds from North Korea-linked Binance hack and disrupts 'FaceStealer' scheme
stories.summary: The Justice Department said more than $2.7 billion of the roughly $6.3 billion stolen from Binance in an Oct. 29 hack has been frozen, and it has court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion. The FBI and Binance attribute the theft to the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor, which officials say is still laundering the remaining funds. Binance says it has fully covered affected customer assets. Officials also announced the disruption of 'FaceStealer,' a scheme that used deepfakes and malicious video-call links to steal more than $400 million over 18 months.
key_facts: Total stolen: about $6.3 billion; more than $2.7 billion frozen; more than $1.2 billion seized or restrained.
Binance says the attack began with a fraudulent job interview that compromised an employee's computer.
The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.
The FBI says North Korea uses stolen crypto to fund its weapons programs.

perspectives.framing: The Record focused on laundering techniques, citing Elliptic and DTEX, and noted that the FBI does not know whether FaceStealer was used in the Binance breach.
Fox Business and the Washington Examiner emphasized the government's rapid response, quoting U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, and Binance's assurance that customers are made whole.

disputed: Whether FaceStealer played any role in the Binance breach is unknown.
How much of the remaining stolen funds can be recovered.
stories.why: This is one of the largest crypto thefts on record, and it is tied to funding for North Korea's weapons programs.

stories.headline: Alaska Airlines to launch daily Charlotte-Seattle nonstop in June 2027
stories.summary: Charlotte Douglas International Airport announced that Alaska Airlines will begin a daily nonstop route to Seattle-Tacoma on June 10, 2027. Alaska will become the ninth airline at the airport. American Airlines already flies the route nonstop.
key_facts: The first flight is June 10, 2027.
The flight arrives in Charlotte at 4:51 p.m. and departs for Seattle at 5:54 p.m. Eastern, taking roughly six hours.

perspectives.framing: Local TV outlets reported it as a straightforward service announcement, quoting the airport's statement on expanded connectivity.

stories.why: It adds another nonstop option and carrier competition for Charlotte travelers.

stories.headline: Korean fashion retailer Musinsa to enter Thailand through Central Retail partnership
stories.summary: Musinsa signed an exclusive distribution deal with Central Marketing Group, part of Thai conglomerate Central Retail, to open Musinsa Standard stores in Thailand. It is Musinsa's fifth Southeast Asian agreement, though no stores have opened yet in the other four markets. No timeline for store openings was given.
key_facts: The agreement was signed Nov. 4.
Musinsa says Thai transaction value on its global online store rose 26% in the first half of the year.
Musinsa operates 49 Musinsa Standard stores in South Korea and plans its first Japan store next year.

perspectives.framing: The Korea Herald and Yonhap reported it as a business expansion story driven by demand for K-fashion. Yonhap noted that the earlier Southeast Asian deals have not yet produced open stores.

disputed: The timeline for opening stores has not been announced.
stories.why: It shows Korean retailers trying to turn the popularity of K-culture into physical stores across Asia.

stories.headline: Former NC lawmaker Jason Saine and ex-Mooresville commissioner David Coble indicted in nonprofit embezzlement case
stories.summary: A Wake County grand jury indicted former Republican state Rep. Jason Saine and former Mooresville commissioner David Coble on felony charges tied to the nonprofit Greater Carolina, Inc. Search warrants say the group's credit card, assigned to Coble, was used at strip club operators, a men's clinic, an Armani store, vacation rentals and other venues, with payments over $400,000. Saine is accused of aiding and abetting rather than embezzlement itself. He denies wrongdoing and says the group's independent board made spending decisions.
key_facts: Saine faces four felony charges; Coble faces five.
The investigation began after an ethics complaint over a 2024 bourbon trip to Kentucky with lawmakers and lobbyists.
Saine helped create Greater Carolina in 2018; Coble was its treasurer.

perspectives.framing: WBTV detailed the search-warrant findings and included Saine's denial in full. WCNC briefly noted Saine's past as a high-ranking lawmaker and the link to the Bourbon Trail probe.

disputed: Saine denies the charges, and Coble's response was not reported in detail.
stories.why: The case raises questions about political nonprofits and how lawmakers are tied to them in North Carolina.
